articles.title: Bengali costs 6.3x the tokens English does — I counted
articles.excerpt: Bengali costs 6.3x the tokens English does — I counted The same paragraph costs 278 tokens in Bengali and 44 in English on Llama 3.1's tokenizer — a 6.3x markup for saying the same thing. On Gemma 3,…
articles.body: Bengali costs 6.3x the tokens English does — I counted The same paragraph costs 278 tokens in Bengali and 44 in English on Llama 3.1's tokenizer — a 6.3x markup for saying the same thing. On Gemma 3, the same paragraph costs 51 tokens in Bengali and 44 in English, a 1.16x markup. The gap is a tokenizer design choice, not physics. The study that sent me counting Last week, University of Michigan researchers published "The Language-Energy Divide" at EMNLP 2026 (DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2113). They ran Qwen 3, Gemma 3, and Meta's Llama 3.1 on reading-comprehension questions from the Belebele dataset in 122 languages, measuring energy with Michigan's ML.Energy framework on the university's Great Lakes cluster.

articles.title: I built a stroke check-in you FaceTime, and the hardest bug wasn't mine
articles.excerpt: The weeks after someone leaves the hospital after a stroke are some of the riskiest of their life. The CDC reports that nearly one in four strokes in the US happen to someone who has already had one.…
articles.body: The weeks after someone leaves the hospital after a stroke are some of the riskiest of their life. The CDC reports that nearly one in four strokes in the US happen to someone who has already had one. After a TIA (a "mini-stroke"), 10 to 15 percent of people have a major stroke within three months, and a lot of that risk lands in the first few weeks. In practice, the early-warning system during those weeks is the family. Somebody's daughter notices that Dad's smile looks a little off at breakfast. Or nobody notices. For Emory Hacks 2026 we built Onset : a one-minute check-in that the patient FaceTimes. No app, no login. Their care team prescribes it for the 90 days after discharge, and each morning the patient calls a phone number and does three things on camera.

articles.title: Giving an AI chat your whole codebase, and getting the changes back without losing your own
articles.excerpt: I use the Claude and ChatGPT web chats on my own projects. Sending the code was never the hard part. Copying the AI's edits back, file by file, without breaking something, was. Here's what I learned d…
articles.body: I use the Claude and ChatGPT web chats on my own projects. Sending the code was never the hard part. Copying the AI's edits back, file by file, without breaking something, was. Here's what I learned doing it safely. 1. Send files, not snippets A model that sees your folder structure guesses less. It finds the files you already have instead of inventing new ones. A ZIP also keeps the paths, so you know where every file in the reply belongs. 2. Leave out the noise Skip dependencies, build output, caches, lockfiles and media. On one of my Next.js projects that's 37,887 of 37,949 files. The 62 left are what a new teammate would actually read. 3. Never send secrets That means .env , private keys, .npmrc , cloud credentials and Terraform state.

articles.title: A Role, Not a Rule
articles.excerpt: At Claude Code Curious in Milton Keynes, one of the organizers made a point I had just run into myself: skills work better written as a role or a metaphor than as detailed instructions. The example wa…
articles.body: At Claude Code Curious in Milton Keynes, one of the organizers made a point I had just run into myself: skills work better written as a role or a metaphor than as detailed instructions. The example was documentation. Instead of listing what good docs contain, ask the model to act as a librarian. The idea is easy to agree with and hard to believe until a rule fails on you. A rule spells out what to do in each case, and a model that follows instructions well applies it to every case that fits, including the ones its author didn't have in mind. A role carries the purpose behind the rule, and the purpose is what tells the cases apart. A librarian knows which documents someone will come looking for. The role depends on the skill. Librarian for documentation; in my case, a colleague.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. articles.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX's Starship megarocket reached orbit today (Nov. 13) during its 15th test flight, but the company scrapped a plan to catch the vehicle's massive booster back at the launch site.
articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
